title: Effect of aspirin on grip strength and gait speed in community-dwelling older adults in the ASPirin in Reducing Events in the Elderly (ASPREE) Study
journal: The Journals of Gerontology Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences

sections.abstract:
Grip strength and gait speed are key markers of physical functional capacity and general health in older people. This study aimed to examine the effect of low-dose aspirin on handgrip strength and habitual gait speed in relatively healthy older people.

The ASPREE (ASPirin in Reducing Events in the Elderly) trial randomized 19 114 community-dwelling Australians and US adults aged 70+ years (US minorities ≥65 years) who were free of overt cardiovascular disease, dementia, and limitations in activities of daily living to daily 100 mg aspirin versus placebo. Linear mixed models were used to compare the effects of treatment groups on changes in grip strength and gait speed over time, and Cox proportional hazard models were used to compare time to incident grip weakness and gait slowness between aspirin and placebo groups.

Over a median of 4.7 years, the changes in grip strength (β: 0.001; 95% CI: −0.004 to 0.005) and gait speed (β: −0.004; 95% CI: −0.010 to 0.001) did not differ significantly between aspirin and placebo groups. Over the study period, 6203 participants experienced incident grip weakness, and 6947 had incident gait slowness. There was no difference in the risk of incident grip weakness (Hazard Ratio (HR): 1.05; 95% CI: 1.00, 1.10) and gait slowness (HR: 1.00; 95% CI: 0.95, 1.05) between individuals randomized to aspirin versus placebo.

Low-dose aspirin use in relatively healthy older people did not affect gait speed or grip strength over time or reduce the risk of weakness and slowness.

Keywords: Aspirin, Clinical trial, Grip strength, Gait speed, Physical functional capacity
sections.introduction:
Age-related declines in muscle strength and mobility are common among older people and are associated with an increased risk of adverse health outcomes, in particular frailty, falls, persistent physical disability, and dementia. 1-3 With global life expectancy increasing, maintaining physical functional independence and mobility among older people has become a public health priority. 4 , 5 Grip strength 6 and gait speed 7 are key objective markers of physical functional capacity and general health in older people. Declines in grip strength and gait speed often signal the early onset of physical disability and frailty, which can lead to loss of independence and reduced quality of life. 2 , 6 , 7

Aging is characterized by inflammaging, which refers to the low-grade chronic inflammation that naturally occurs as people age, even in the absence of illness or infection. 8-10 Effective pharmacological interventions targeting inflammation could thus help preserve or improve physical functioning that declines with age, such as slower gait speed and reduced grip strength. This, in turn, could help delay the incidence of disability and frailty. Aspirin, an archetypal nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug, has been recognized for its dual actions (antithrombotic and anti-inflammatory effects). 11 , 12 Aspirin inhibits platelet-derived thromboxane A2 synthesis, thereby providing its antithrombotic effects by reducing thrombus formation on the arterial wall surface. 11 , 12 Thus, through its antithrombotic effects, aspirin could support vascular health, thereby promoting efficient oxygen and nutrient delivery to skeletal muscle, which in turn helps to maintain mobility and muscle strength. 13 Additionally, through inhibition of the cyclooxygenase (COX) pathway of arachidonic acid metabolism, aspirin achieves its anti-inflammatory effects by reducing the production of inflammatory prostaglandin (PGs). 11 , 12 Furthermore, prolonged COX inhibition attenuates systemic inflammation by lowering the levels of pro-inflammatory markers, such as interleukin-6 (IL-6) and C-reactive protein (CRP), 14 which are key contributors to age-related declines in physical strength and disability among older people. 9 , 15–17 Therefore, investigating the potential effects of low-dose aspirin on physical functioning, specifically grip strength and gait speed, could provide new insights into its potential benefits for maintaining mobility and preventing disability in late life, beyond its traditional uses.

The ASPirin in Reducing Events in the Elderly (ASPREE) was a randomized, placebo-controlled trial that established that low-dose aspirin does not affect disability-free survival when used in primary prevention among older adults. 18 ASPREE also determined that low-dose aspirin does not reduce the risk of incident frailty 19 ; however, there was some evidence that it may reduce persistent physical disability, although it did not reach significance over the trial’s median follow-up period of 4.7 years. 20 , 21 Changes in grip strength and gait speed are early indicators of declining physical functioning. The effect of aspirin could be found in more subtle changes in these indicators. These physical functioning indicators may thus provide a more sensitive measure of aspirin’s effect. Therefore, this study aimed to examine the effect of low-dose daily aspirin use on handgrip strength and habitual gait speed in healthy older people enrolled in the ASPREE study.
sections.methods:
ASPREE was approved by multiple Institutional Review Boards in the United States and Australia ( www.aspree.org ), registered with the International Standard Randomized Controlled Trial Number Register (ISRCTN83772183) and clinicaltrials.gov ( NCT01038583 ) and undertaken in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.

The ASPREE study included 19 114 initially healthy community-dwelling individuals. Recruitment occurred from March 2010 through December 2014 in Australia ( n = 16 703) and the United States ( n = 2411). 18 , 22 In Australia, participants were recruited through general practice, whereas in the United States, recruitment took place predominantly through clinical trials and academic centers. Eligible participants were community-dwelling individuals aged ≥70 years (or aged ≥65 years for US minority—African American or Hispanic groups). 18 Detailed descriptions of the exclusion criteria have been published previously. 18 In brief, individuals were excluded if they had a history of a diagnosed cardiovascular disease (CVD) (ie, stroke, myocardial infarction, unstable angina, heart failure, transient ischemic attack, coronary artery reperfusion procedures and bypass grafting, and abdominal aortic aneurysm); a clinical diagnosis of atrial fibrillation; a diagnosis of dementia or a score of <78 on the Modified Mini-Mental State Examination; substantial physical activity limitations (ie, severe difficulty or unable to perform any of 6 basic activities of daily living [ADL]); a condition with high risk of major bleeding; anemia; uncontrolled hypertension (ie, a systolic blood pressure ≥180 mmHg and/or a diastolic blood pressure ≥ 105 mmHg); a serious illness likely to cause death within the next 5 years as perceived by the recruiting general practitioner; and were currently using aspirin (and unwilling to stop) or other antiplatelet or antithrombotic medication.

Details of the randomization and study measurements were described in the ASPREE protocol 23 available at www.aspree.org . In brief, eligible participants were enrolled in a 4-week run-in phase, during which adherence to placebo tablets was monitored; the identity of these tablets was not disclosed to the participants. Participants with ≥80% compliance were randomly assigned to receive a 100 mg enteric-coated aspirin tablet daily or a matching enteric-coated placebo tablet in a ratio of 1:1. 18 ASPREE used block randomization with a computer-generated randomization procedure in STATA statistical software. The randomization list was generated using the STATA “ralloc” procedure with randomization stratified according to location of general practice in Australia, regional site in the United States, and age (65-79 or ≥80 years), which ensured balanced allocation across groups. The randomization list was generated by an independent statistician and was inaccessible to all of the ASPREE study staff and senior investigators. Study participants, investigators, and general practitioner coinvestigators were blinded to treatment allocation.

Medication compliance was assessed using annual pill counts from returned bottles. Participants who ceased study medication for any reason were encouraged to remain on the trial and continue attending annual visits for event monitoring and data collection. The ASPREE intervention phase was concluded in June 2017. 20

The ASPREE trial was powered for its primary outcome of disability-free survival (a composite of dementia, physical disability, or death). The sample size calculations for the primary and secondary endpoints were reported previously. 23 , 24 Given a total sample size of >19 000, we have 90% power to detect a hazard ratio of 1.23 comparing the aspirin group with placebo in an intention-to-treat analysis, where compliance with medication and dropout are assumed as for the primary endpoint. 23 , 24 Analysis of the present study was undertaken on an intention-to-treat basis. Thus, given the large sample size, the current analyses remain well-powered to detect clinically meaningful differences between treatment arms.

Handgrip strength and habitual gait speed were measured by trained staff at baseline and face-to-face follow-up visits (years 2, 4, 6, and 7 or close-out visits, which could correspond to years 3 to 7. 3

Handgrip strength in kilograms of force was assessed using an isometric handheld dynamometer (Jamar; Lafayette Instruments). ASPREE staff checked dynamometers weekly to ensure consistency, replacing any devices that showed a high degree of variation. Calibration was conducted annually by weighing a 5-pound weight bag in the United States and by a validated servicing agent in Australia. The assessments were undertaken according to the American Society of Hand Therapists (ASHT) protocol. 25 Full details regarding the handgrip strength assessment in ASPREE have been described in detail previously. 3 Participants completed a maximum of 3 trials on each hand with a 15- to 20-second rest in between. The mean score for each participant’s self-reported dominant hand was used in the analysis. 3

Gait speed was assessed as the time spent walking 3 m at the participant’s habitual walking pace indoors on a flat surface from a standing start. A minimum of an additional 1-m spare space was provided at the end of the course to ensure a habitual pace, which they maintained over the full course of 3 m. 3 Gait speed (total seconds for 3 m) was measured twice, and the mean score was used in the analysis. Notably, the 3-m walk test has been demonstrated to provide a valid and strongly correlated measure with the longer 6-m walk test, 23 , 26 serving as a practical and reliable alternative for assessing gait speed in large-scale community-based studies and general practice settings where long hallways are often unavailable. 23

Intention-to-treat analyses were used to examine the effects of aspirin versus placebo on (1) change in grip strength or gait speed over time and (2) incident grip weakness or gait slowness during the intervention phase of ASPREE (from enrollment to June 12, 2017).

First, linear mixed models were also used to compare the effects of treatment groups on changes in grip strength and gait speed over time. The models assume that data are missing at random (MAR). The Z -scores (standardized scores) of grip strength at each time point were calculated using the mean and SD of baseline grip strength scores specific to each sex- and BMI-specific category. 27 The sex- and BMI-specific categories were presented in Table S1 . The Z -scores of gait speed at each time point were estimated using the mean and SD of baseline gait speed scores specific to each sex and height-specific category. 27 The sex and height-specific categories were presented in Table S2 . These BMI and height cutoffs correspond to the Cardiovascular Health Study definitions and operationalization for the Frailty phenotype. 3 , 27 Each model included a participant-specific random intercept and random slope, and treatment group (aspirin vs placebo) by time (annual visits: 0, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7) interaction to quantify the effect of treatment group on changes in grip strength or gait speed over time. Subgroup analyses were also performed according to the prespecified subgroups (as published in the statistical analysis plan of the ASPREE study). 20 , 24

Next, Cox proportional-hazards regression models were used to examine the effects of randomized treatment (aspirin vs placebo) on incident grip weakness and gait slowness separately. Grip weakness was defined based on the lowest 20% grip strength at baseline within sex and BMI-specific categories (described in Table S1 ). 3 , 27 The specific cutoff values used to define weakness for each sex and BMI-specific categories are presented in Table S3 . Incident grip weakness was identified at the first annual visit, where their grip strength met the criteria for weakness. Gait slowness was defined as the slowest 20% at baseline within sex- and height-specific categories (described in Table S2 ). 3 , 27 The specific cutoff values used to define slowness for each sex and height-specific categories are presented in Table S4 . Incident gait slowness was identified at the first annual visit, where their gait speed met the criteria for slowness. Of note, our approach to defining weakness and slowness based on the lowest 20% of grip strength and slowest 20% of gait speed at baseline, adjusted for sex, and BMI or height, follows the method used to operationalize the Fried Frailty Phenotype. 27 Further, our cutoffs for men’s and women’s grip weakness and gait slowness, specific to each sex and body-size-specific category, are closely aligned with those used by both the European Working Group on Sarcopenia in Older People and the Asian Working Group for Sarcopenia. 28 Moreover, our grip weakness cutoff values are broadly consistent with international norms for handgrip strength levels of the weakest 20% among older adults, representing 69 countries and regions. 29 Time to event in these Cox models was defined as the date of the annual visit at which the participant first met the criteria for incident weakness/slowness during the trial period (at which time point they were censored), or in the absence of an event, the date of the last annual visit when weakness/slowness was assessed. Testing of proportional hazard assumptions in survival analyses was undertaken using Schoenfeld residuals, with all p values found to be >.1, indicating no significant evidence of a violation of the proportional hazard assumption. The cumulative incidence curves for each outcome stratified according to the aspirin and placebo groups were also generated. In addition, the analyses were repeated with the consideration of a competing risk of death in the Cox proportional-hazards models. Of note, the cumulative incidence of death during follow-up was low (<5%). Subgroup analyses were also undertaken to determine the effect of aspirin versus placebo on incident outcomes according to the ASPREE trial’s prespecified subgroups (as published in the statistical analysis plan of the ASPREE study). 20 , 24 Furthermore, given that our time-to-event data were collected at follow-up study visits in discrete intervals, sensitivity analyses were also conducted using Discrete-Time Survival Analysis (through applying the Generalized Linear Model with binomial family and complementary log-log link function with eform), checking whether our observed associations on the effects of aspirin on incident outcomes were consistent when using Discrete-Time Survival Analysis. All analyses were undertaken using STATA version 17.0 (StataCorp, College Station, TX, United States) and R version 4.1.3.
sections.results:
A total of 19 114 participants (56.4% women) aged 65-98 years were included in this trial and underwent randomization (9525 participants to the aspirin group and 9589 to the placebo group, Table 1 ). The majority (85.6%) were White Australians, and the median age of the participants was 74 years in both the aspirin and placebo groups.

Diabetes mellitus is defined from self-report or fasting glucose ≥ 126 mg/dL (≥7 mmol/L) or on treatment for diabetes mellitus; Hypertension is defined as “on treatment” for high BP or BP > 140/90 mmHg at study entry; Dyslipidemia defined as those taking cholesterol-lowering medications or serum cholesterol ≥212 mg/dL (≥5.5 mmol/L; Australia) and ≥240 mg/dL (≥6.2 mmol/L; United States) or LDL > 160 mg/dL (>4.1 mmol/L).

The medication compliance rate was 73% for those in the aspirin group and 74% for those in the placebo group throughout the trial period. 19 Adverse events (AEs) or serious adverse events (SAEs) have been reported in our previous papers. 20 , 30 , 31 SAEs were part of the main disability-free survival outcome, 20 and mortality was also examined separately. 30 Bleeding event, which is the AE directly related to aspirin use, was described previously. 31

Over a median of 4.7 years, there was no evidence of a difference in the average trajectories of grip strength overall between the aspirin and placebo groups (β: 0.001; 95% CI: −0.004 to 0.005, Figures 1 and 2 ). The associations differed by ethno-racial groups ( p -interaction = .04), with the aspirin group being associated with better grip strength over time among Hispanics/Latinos (β: 0.037; 95% CI: 0.002 to 0.072, Figure 2 ). No significant associations were found in other subgroup analyses ( Figure 2 and Table S5 ).

Estimated marginal means of (A) grip strength and (B) gait speed scores over follow-up according to the aspirin and placebo groups.

Forest plot of subgroup analyses on the effects of aspirin versus placebo on mean change in grip strength (standardized Z scores) over time. Positive beta values indicate an increase in the grip strength over time in the aspirin group compared to the placebo group; negative beta values indicate a decrease in the grip strength over time in the aspirin group compared to the placebo group; the vertical line at 0 represents no difference between groups. BMI, body mass index.

Similarly, there was no evidence of a difference in the average trajectories of gait speed overall between aspirin and placebo groups (β: −0.004; 95% CI: −0.010 to 0.001, Figures 1 and 3 ). The effect of aspirin on gait speed trajectories varied across BMI categories ( p -interaction = .01). Aspirin was associated with worse gait speed over time among individuals with normal weight (β: −0.016; 95% CI: −0.027 to −0.005, Figure 3 ) compared to normal-weight individuals in the placebo group. No significant associations were found in other subgroups ( Figure 3 and Table S6 ).

Forest plot of subgroup analyses on the effects of aspirin versus placebo on mean change in gait speed (standardized Z scores) over time. Positive beta values indicate an increase in the gait speed over time in the aspirin group compared to the placebo group; negative beta values indicate a decrease in the gait speed over time in the aspirin group compared to the placebo group; the vertical line at 0 represents no difference between groups. BMI, body mass index.

Over a median of 4.7 years, 6203 participants experienced incident grip weakness, comprising 3138 (98.4 events per 1000-person years) from the aspirin group and 3065 (93.9 events per 1000-person years) from the placebo group. There were 6947 participants who had incident gait slowness, with 3446 cases (108.3 events per 1000-person years) occurring in the aspirin group and 3501 cases (108.5 events per 1000-person years) in the placebo group. There was no difference in the risk of incident grip weakness (HR: 1.05; 95% CI: 1.00 to 1.10) or gait slowness (HR: 1.00; 95% CI: 0.95 to 1.05) between individuals randomized to aspirin versus placebo ( Figure 4 ). Similar results were observed when considering the competing risk of death in the models (HR: 1.04; 95% CI 0.99 to 1.09 for incident grip weakness, and HR: 0.99; 95% CI 0.95 to 1.04 for incident gait slowness). Further, the results were the same ( Table S7 ) when applying the Generalized Linear Model (Discrete Time Survival Analysis).

Cumulative incidence of (A) grip weakness and (B) gait slowness according to the aspirin and placebo groups. HR, hazard ratio.

There was no evidence of a differential effect of aspirin on the risk of grip weakness in any subgroup analysis ( p -interaction > .3, Figure S1 [see online supplementary material for a color version of this figure] and Table S8 ). The effect of aspirin on incident gait slowness differed across the ethno-racial groups ( p -interaction = .01, Figure S2 [see online supplementary material for a color version of this figure]). A lower risk of incident gait slowness was observed in the aspirin group among African Americans (HR: 0.84; 95% CI: 0.71 to 0.99) and Hispanics/Latinos (HR: 0.72; 95% CI: 0.55 to 0.96). No evidence of a differential effect of aspirin on the risk of incident gait slowness was found in any other subgroups ( p -interaction > .1, Figure S2 [see online supplementary material for a color version of this figure] and Table S9 ).
sections.discussion:
The primary findings of the ASPREE trial demonstrated that initiating low-dose aspirin in late life has no significant effect on the prevention of frailty, 19 disability-free survival, 20 cardiovascular events, 31 and dementia, 32 but showed some evidence of an effect on reducing persistent physical disability measured as loss of basic ADL ability. 20 , 21 The present study extends these initial findings, examining the effect of aspirin on the physical function measures of grip strength and gait speed. This study found no statistically significant difference in the longitudinal changes in grip strength and gait speed over time between the 2 treatment groups. The incidence rate of grip weakness was slightly higher in the aspirin treatment group (98.4 per 1000 person-years) compared to the placebo group (93.9 per 1000 person-years), while the incidence rate of gait slowness was similar in both the aspirin and placebo treatment groups. However, we found no difference in the risk of developing grip weakness or gait slowness between individuals taking low-dose aspirin and those taking a placebo over a median of 4.7 years of follow-up.

It is known that aspirin reduces the production of inflammatory PGs by inhibiting the COX pathway of arachidonic acid metabolism, thereby providing its anti-inflammatory effects. 11 , 12 Prolonged COX inhibition has been shown to attenuate the levels of pro-inflammatory markers, such as IL-6 and CRP. 14 However, evidence on the extent to which low-dose aspirin modulates the levels of pro-inflammatory markers such as IL-6 and CRP is mixed and remains inconclusive. While the effect of aspirin on IL-6 appears to be less consistent, some studies found modest reductions in CRP. 33-35 Given that IL-6 and CRP are key pro-inflammatory markers involved in age-related decline in muscle strength, 9 , 15-17 the inconsistent evidence raises questions about whether aspirin has a meaningful anti-inflammatory effect in the context of age-related functional decline. Previous cohort studies have reported mixed findings on the effect of daily aspirin or NSAID use on muscle health. 36-38 A cross-sectional study observed that chronic COX inhibition via aspirin did not influence age‐related skeletal muscle atrophy, 36 whereas prospective cohort studies conducted among male physicians showed that long-term aspirin use started in middle age was associated with a higher likelihood of faster walking speed in late life, 37 and long-term use of NSAIDs at high frequency was associated with a greater risk of frailty. 38 Notably, low-dose aspirin, primarily known for its antiplatelet effects, has an established safety profile and is among the most widely used agents for cardiovascular prevention among older adults. 23 , 39 Based on this, along with its anti-inflammatory action, 11 , 12 , 14 it was hypothesized that low-dose aspirin could support muscle strength. Our current null findings may reflect the limited anti-inflammatory action of low-dose aspirin use, which primarily exerts an antiplatelet effect rather than an anti-inflammatory action. 11 , 40-42 However, given that our study examined the effect of low-dose aspirin only, our findings do not provide direct evidence to conclude whether higher doses are more effective, nor do they support the dose-dependent nature of aspirin’s anti-inflammatory effect. Besides, the underlying mechanisms behind age-related declines in physical strength are likely to be multifactorial, involving not only inflammation but also hormonal, neuromuscular decline, social, nutritional, and other lifestyle-related factors, including regular exercise; thus, low-dose aspirin alone may not completely address all these contributors to physical health over time. Given that low grip strength and slow gait speed are key indicators of loss of physical ability and other health outcomes among older adults, further research is warranted to investigate the impact of another pharmacological approach, either alone or in combination with lifestyle-based interventions, on preserving physical ability in aging populations.

In our subgroup analysis, we found that among older people with normal weight, individuals who took low-dose aspirin showed a decline in gait speed over time compared to those not taking aspirin. This result raises a question about the potential side effects of long-term, low-dose aspirin intake on physical mobility among relatively healthy older people within the normal weight range, suggesting further investigation into this relationship and its underlying mechanisms. One of the possible explanations for this finding could be related to aspirin’s anti-inflammatory effects, 11 , 12 which could have unintended consequences for the musculoskeletal system. For example, as noted above, aspirin’s anti-inflammatory effects through inhibition of the COX pathway, which in turn reduces the production of inflammatory PGs, 11 , 12 may affect the role of PGs in the regeneration of muscle repair biology. 43 Thus, although long-term aspirin use may have a beneficial effect in reducing systemic inflammation, its chronic suppression of inflammation through reducing PGs production may negatively affect muscle function and joint health over time. In addition, levels of systemic inflammation are found to be lower among normal-weight individuals compared to those who are overweight or obese. 44 Consequently, it is possible that the negative impact of chronic aspirin use on gait speed may be more pronounced among those within the normal weight range and with lower levels of systemic inflammation. Further, given that there is potential for type 1 errors with multiple comparisons, caution is needed when interpreting the results of our subgroup analyses.

The present study found a significant interaction effect between low-dose aspirin use and ethno-racial groups, with African Americans and Hispanics/Latinos possibly benefiting from aspirin use in reducing the risk of developing gait slowness over time. In addition, we also observed that long-term low-dose aspirin use among Hispanics/Latinos was associated with sustained handgrip strength over time. These findings suggest potential ethno-racial differences in the benefits of low-dose aspirin on physical functioning capabilities. Prior studies reported that Hispanics/Latinos experience the highest burden of metabolic syndrome, which includes hypertension, high blood sugar, and excess body fat around the waist 45 ; these conditions that severely undermine skeletal muscle strength. 46 It is known that a systemic inflammatory condition plays a central role in the pathophysiology of metabolic syndrome. 47 Thus, the anti-inflammatory effects of low-dose aspirin use may perhaps mitigate some detrimental effects of metabolic syndrome, thereby contributing to preserving physical functioning capabilities in this ethno-racial group. In addition, prior research has revealed differences in aspirin responsiveness across ethno-racial groups, potentially due to genetic and metabolic factors. 48-50 Such variability could also help explain our observed benefits in gait speed and grip strength among African Americans and Hispanics/Latinos. So, our findings on ethno-racial differences suggest that further investigation is warranted to validate these findings in a large sample of African American and Hispanic/Latino populations.

Our study had both strengths and limitations. The main strength stems from our randomized trial design: a placebo-controlled double-blind clinical trial in a large community-based cohort of older people. 22 Another strength of our study is that we assessed grip strength and gait speed at multiple time points over 5 years, and these assessments were administered by trained staff following strict standard operational procedures. By employing both the linear mixed model and the Cox model, this study enables a thorough examination of both the trajectories of physical functioning and the onset of physical performance decline, effectively capturing its dynamic nature across the study period. This dual approach provides a comprehensive analysis of the effects of low-dose aspirin on physical functional capacity in late life (ie, grip strength and gait speed). One limitation is that approximately 90% of our study participants were White Australians and Americans. This could affect the generalizability of our present findings to other specific ethno-racial groups, including Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islanders, Native Americans, and Asians. However, our population included a substantial number of African Americans and Hispanic/Latinos, in addition to White Australians and Americans. Our sample had good distribution in terms of gender (women, 56%), education level (eg, 45% had <12 years of education), and socioeconomic status (about one-third living in socioeconomically disadvantaged areas). In addition, our ASPREE study cohort is largely representative of community-dwelling older Australians (49% living in regional or rural areas) and older Americans (mostly located in the Midwest and East Coast). 22 Furthermore, we acknowledge that, as part of the inclusion and exclusion criterion, ASPREE excluded individuals with existing indications for aspirin or other antithrombotic agents. This is because of ethical concerns, as randomizing those individuals would have put them at risk of being assigned to the placebo group. So, our cohort is likely to have a healthier vascular profile, and thus our findings may not fully generalize to older adults at higher vascular risk. Additionally, it is recognized that the medication adherence in our ASPREE trial was moderate (ie, 73% for the aspirin group and 74% for the placebo group), with comparable rates between the two groups, thereby reducing the likelihood that differential adherence biased the findings. Moreover, we note that our ASPREE recruitment occurred from 2010 to 2014, and the trial concluded in June 2017. Thus, with a median follow-up of 4.7 years across the cohort, only participants enrolled earlier (ie, in 2010) had up to 7 years of follow-up, whereas those enrolled in 2014 had about 3 years of follow-up. Furthermore, in-person assessments of grip strength and gait speed were conducted at baseline and at follow-up years 2, 4, 6, and 7, or at the close-out visit, which corresponds to years 3 to 7. As such, fewer participants contributed data in years 3 and 7 due to the staggered recruitment and trial close-out schedule.

sections.conclusion: In summary, our study found that taking low-dose aspirin among older people was not associated with significant changes in grip strength and gait speed over time and did not reduce the risk of grip weakness or gait slowness over a median of 4.7 years of follow-up. These findings suggest that low-dose aspirin did not benefit the maintenance of physical functioning among relatively healthy older people, further adding to our previous null findings for aspirin in preventing frailty, depression, dementia, and CVD events in the ASPREE study.
